You are given one person (a thinker), the lead section of their encyclopedia article (EXTRACT), and a list of historical events and periods whose dates overlap the person's life (EVENTS, each with an id).

Say which of the listed events bear on this person, and how. Use only the EXTRACT: if the extract does not mention or clearly imply an event, do not connect it, even if you know the connection from elsewhere. An event that merely happened during the person's life is not a connection unless the extract brings it up.

For each connection give:
- "event": the id from the EVENTS list, exactly as written (Q followed by digits). Never an event that is not in the list.
- "type", one of:
  - "lived_through": the extract mentions the event as part of the person's circumstances, without saying they acted in it or wrote against it;
  - "took_part_in": the person acted in the event (fought, sat in the assembly, negotiated, signed, governed, led);
  - "wrote_in_response_to": a named work, or the person's writing generally, answers or treats the event; put the work's title in "work" if the extract names one;
  - "suffered_under": the person was exiled, imprisoned, censored, dismissed, persecuted or killed because of the event;
  - "shaped_by": the extract says the event formed the person's thinking, without naming a work.
- "reason": one sentence in your own words.
- "evidence": one sentence copied exactly from the EXTRACT, character for character, that supports the connection. Do not paraphrase, shorten or join sentences.
- "work": the title of the work, if the type is wrote_in_response_to and the extract names it; otherwise an empty string.

If an event in the list is the same thing under a broader or narrower name as one the extract mentions (the extract says "the civil war" and the list has "English Civil War"), connect it. If nothing in the extract bears on any listed event, return an empty list. Return JSON only, matching the schema you are given.

PERSON: Peter Abelard (1079–1142-04-28). French scholastic philosopher, theologian and preeminent logician (c.1079-1142)

EXTRACT:
Peter Abelard (12 February 1079 – 21 April 1142) was a French philosopher, logician, theologian, composer, and poet, regarded as one of the most brilliant and controversial theologians of his time. Born at Pallet, near Nantes, he became a popular lecturer in Paris, but his academic career was cut short after his love affair with his student and eventual wife, Héloïse d'Argenteuil. Their relationship and philosophical exchange later became the aspect of his life for which he is best known in history and popular culture.
In philosophy, Abelard challenged the prevailing philosophical orthodoxy and is celebrated for his logical treatment of the problem of universals through nominalism and conceptualism, thereby helping to prepare the way for nominalism, as well as for pioneering the role of intent in ethics. He has often been called the "Descartes of the twelfth century" and has been considered a forerunner of Rousseau, Kant, and Spinoza. He is also sometimes credited as a major forerunner of modern empiricism.
In Catholic theology, Abelard was condemned for his teaching on the Trinity. He is particularly known for developing the concept of limbo and for introducing the moral influence theory of atonement. His doctrine of the atonement emphasized the love of Christ as manifested in his life and Passion, which in turn calls forth a human response of love, and this conception has had a continuing influence. Abelard expressed its underlying purpose in the words: "The purpose and cause of the incarnation was that God might illuminate the world by his wisdom and stir it to the love of himself."
Abelard is also regarded, alongside Augustine, as one of the most significant forerunners of the modern self-reflective autobiographer. His publicly circulated autobiographical letter, The History of My Calamities, together with his public correspondence, helped establish the tone for later epistolary novels and public accounts of the private lives of prominent figures. His works also include Christian Theology, Ethics, and his letters to Héloïse.
